subject: english-language
promptStrong: Give me an exam-style {board} {level} {subject} question on {lo}, then mark my answer against the mark scheme.
promptWeak: Explain {lo} for {board} {level} {subject} simply, with a clear example and the most common mistake students make.

questions.q: Which sentence best uses 'show, not tell' to convey that a character is nervous?
options: The girl was nervous because of the test.
She felt nervous and scared inside.
She was very nervous about the exam.
Her hands trembled as she gripped the pencil, her eyes fixed on the clock.
questions.explain: Showing physical detail lets the reader infer the emotion rather than stating it outright.

questions.q: "The medicine cured nine out of ten patients in the trial." In a health article, this statement is best classed as a:
questions.explain: A trial result expressed as a verifiable figure is a fact, not a judgement.

questions.q: "The forest was a cathedral of green." The comparison of the forest to a cathedral mainly creates a sense of:
questions.explain: A cathedral connotes height, quiet and awe, so the metaphor lends the forest grandeur and reverence.

questions.q: Which is the best way to adapt your writing for a young child as the audience?
options: Use long, complex sentences and abstract vocabulary
Use simple, clear sentences, friendly tone and concrete vocabulary
Include dense statistics and technical jargon
Write in a formal, legalistic register
questions.explain: Writing for young children needs simple sentences, a warm tone and accessible words.

questions.q: A dove is used throughout a text to represent peace. Using an object to stand for an idea is:
questions.explain: An object standing for a larger idea (a dove for peace) is symbolism.

questions.q: A writer follows a long, flowing description with the single line: "Everything stopped." Standing alone as its own paragraph, this short sentence creates:
options: A sudden pause and dramatic emphasis
questions.explain: An isolated short sentence after long ones forces a pause and lands with dramatic impact.

questions.q: A writer's TONE in "Honestly, what a complete and utter shambles this has become" is best described as:
questions.explain: The dismissive phrasing conveys scorn and frustration.

questions.q: "Do we really want our children breathing this filthy air?" Which technique is this?
questions.explain: It is a question asked for effect, not for an answer: a rhetorical question.

questions.q: "Year after year, ton after ton, our oceans drown in plastic." The repetition of "after" mainly works to:
options: Stress the relentless, ongoing scale of the problem
questions.explain: Repeating "after" emphasises a continuous, mounting build-up, stressing the scale.

questions.q: What is the best way to structure a piece of persuasive writing for impact?
options: Save the main point for a footnote
Open with a hook, develop arguments in clear paragraphs, end with a memorable call to action
Put every idea in one giant paragraph
List random facts in no order
questions.explain: A strong structure hooks, develops logically and ends with a powerful closing message.

questions.q: Which of these is a FACT rather than an opinion?
options: This is the best film ever made
The film is too long and dull
questions.explain: A runtime can be checked and verified, making it a fact; the others are judgements.

questions.q: What is the main purpose of a discourse marker such as 'however' or 'furthermore'?
options: To signal the relationship between ideas and guide the reader
questions.explain: Discourse markers connect ideas and show contrast, addition or sequence to aid coherence.

questions.q: Early in a story, a character nervously eyes a loaded gun on the wall. Hinting at a later event is:
questions.explain: Planting an early hint of something to come is foreshadowing.

questions.q: A columnist writes: "Of course, some will say the scheme is too costly. But can we really put a price on safety?" This technique of raising and then dismissing the opposing view is:
questions.explain: Acknowledging an objection and then countering it is a counter-argument or rebuttal.

questions.q: A writer's TONE in "I suppose, if one absolutely must, one could call this 'art'" is best described as:
questions.explain: The reluctant phrasing and scare-quotes around "art" convey sarcasm and dismissal.

questions.q: A speech opens and closes with the very same phrase, "We will not be moved." Framing a text this way is best described as:
questions.explain: Beginning and ending with the same idea creates a cyclical (circular) structure.

questions.q: Which sentence is a SIMPLE sentence (one main clause)?
options: The dog barked and the cat ran.
When she arrived, the show began, although it was late.
Because it rained, we stayed in.
questions.explain: "The dog barked." has a single main clause, making it a simple sentence.

questions.q: "This shameful, disgraceful waste of money makes me furious." The underlined choices are best described as:
questions.explain: Words chosen to stir strong feeling (shameful, disgraceful, furious) are emotive language.

questions.q: "It was cruel, heartless and utterly inhumane." The use of three linked words for emphasis is called:
questions.explain: Three items grouped for rhetorical force is tripling (a triplet/rule of three).

questions.q: A leaflet tells readers "Always wear a helmet and check your brakes." Its main purpose is to:
questions.explain: Practical guidance and instructions for the reader's benefit show the purpose is to advise.

questions.q: "Her smile was as bright as the sun." This is an example of a:
questions.explain: A comparison using "as" is a simile.

questions.q: Identifying a writer's VIEWPOINT means working out:
options: Their attitude or opinion towards the subject
questions.explain: Viewpoint is the writer's stance or attitude on the topic.
